title: A day in Pompeii
status: Source-informed educational prototype; not yet reviewed by a Pompeii specialist or aligned to a specific school assessment standard.
mission: What can ordinary objects tell us about unequal lives in Pompeii? Collect evidence from a home, a food counter and a workplace. Explain one difference, then identify what the evidence cannot tell you.
sceneLabel: Composite reconstruction. Inspired by documented Pompeian features; not a measured model of one ancient street or building.

hotspots.title: A street you can read
hotspots.documented: The Archaeological Park describes raised oval stones linking the pavements on Via dell’Abbondanza. The shaped road helped water drain, while the stones helped pedestrians cross without getting wet.
hotspots.interpretation: Look at the relationship between the road and the crossing. It suggests how people managed everyday movement and water. Our arrangement is illustrative, not a survey of that street.
hotspots.question: Why might the crossing sit above the road surface?
hotspots.sourceLabel: Pompeii Archaeological Park · Along the streets of Pompeii
hotspots.takeaway: Even a crossing is evidence of daily life.

hotspots.title: Lunch on the street
hotspots.documented: Thermopolia served food and drink. Large jars called dolia were built into masonry counters. The excavated Regio V example preserves a painted counter and containers.
hotspots.interpretation: A food counter helps us investigate eating outside the home. The containers shown here do not establish the exact menu, prices or customers of this imagined shop.
hotspots.question: What does a built-in food container tell us? What does it leave unknown?
hotspots.sourceLabel: Pompeii Archaeological Park · Thermopolium of Regio V
hotspots.takeaway: An object can support a claim without answering every question.

hotspots.title: Who made the bread?
hotspots.documented: Pompeian bakeries preserve lava millstones and ovens. At one excavated bakery in Regio IX, archaeologists found restricted access, barred openings and cuts in the floor around the mills.
hotspots.interpretation: The excavators interpret that enclosed workplace as evidence of enslaved people and animals being confined and exploited. This does not establish the status of every bakery worker. A comfortable city depended on labour that was not equally free.
hotspots.question: How does evidence from a workplace change the story told by a wealthy home?
hotspots.sourceLabel: Pompeii Archaeological Park · Regio IX bakery excavation, 2023 (Italian)

additionalSources.label: Official excavation guide · House of the Oven, printed page 62

hotspots.evidenceType: Excavated equipment and interpretation of restricted movement
hotspots.takeaway: Remember the people whose work supported daily life.

hotspots.title: Rain becomes a resource
hotspots.documented: In an atrium house, rain entered through the roof opening, the compluvium. A basin below, the impluvium, collected it and channelled water into an underground cistern for household use.
hotspots.interpretation: This house represents one form of comfortable domestic architecture. Pompeii also had much smaller, simpler homes. Its water system should not be treated as every resident’s experience.
hotspots.question: Follow the rain: where would it go after reaching the basin?
hotspots.takeaway: A beautiful room can also be practical technology.

hotspots.title: Walls that say something
hotspots.documented: The House of the Vettii preserves richly decorated rooms. Its painted Cupids take part in activities including wine selling, cloth cleaning and perfume making.
hotspots.interpretation: Decoration can suggest wealth, interests and self-presentation. Painted scenes are designed images, not photographs of work. The colours and pattern in this prototype are newly authored, not a copy of a particular surviving fresco.
hotspots.question: What might a decorated room communicate to a visitor? Why should we read its images critically?
hotspots.sourceLabel: Pompeii Archaeological Park · House of the Vettii
hotspots.takeaway: Art tells us about choices as well as activities.

hotspots.title: A jar with a journey
hotspots.documented: The Boscoreale Antiquarium displays transport amphorae for wine and oil, and a fragment with traces of fish sauce. One fruit amphora carries a painted inscription describing apples from Cumae.
hotspots.interpretation: Container shapes, labels and residues help researchers investigate goods and exchange. This unlabelled model cannot tell us its own contents or route: those need evidence.
hotspots.question: Which would make a stronger claim about a jar’s contents: its colour, an inscription, or a surviving residue?
hotspots.sourceLabel: Pompeii Archaeological Park · Boscoreale Antiquarium, Room I
hotspots.takeaway: Small finds can connect a household to a wider world.

assessment.question: What was the impluvium designed to do?
options: Collect rainwater entering through the roof
Store food inside a shop counter
assessment.explanation: The basin collected rainwater and channelled it into a cistern. Follow the water path from roof to basin to storage.

assessment.question: Which conclusion is best supported by the home and bakery evidence together?
options: Every Pompeian enjoyed a large decorated home
Comfort and working conditions differed between people
Every person working in a bakery was enslaved
assessment.explanation: Decorated houses and evidence of controlled labour reveal different experiences. One building cannot represent everyone, and one bakery cannot establish every worker’s status.

assessment.question: A detailed 3D scene shows an amphora filled with wine. What makes that a historical claim we can trust?
options: Relevant finds or records support the contents, and uncertainty is stated
assessment.explanation: Realism is a visual quality, not evidence. Inscriptions, residues and research can support a reconstruction; missing information should remain visible.

reflection.prompt: Was daily life in Pompeii the same for everyone?
reflection.instructions: Use at least two discoveries. Explain what each supports, and name one thing you still cannot know.
scaffold: A different experience is shown by…
reflection.feedback: Self-review: have you named evidence, explained your inference, and included a limitation? This prototype does not automatically grade your historical argument.

limitations: This is a composite, newly authored reconstruction. It is not a measured digital twin, archaeological survey, licensed photogrammetry capture or historical photograph.
Locations, dimensions, colours, movable objects and arrangements are illustrative unless a hotspot explicitly identifies supporting evidence.
Any rebuilt or remains-style view is an interpretation of this model, not a comparison with a scanned present-day site.
The scene represents daily life before the eruption of AD 79; it does not specify the disputed calendar date of the eruption.
No fictional dialogue, exact prices or invented personal biographies are presented as historical records.
Archaeological interpretation can change. The Regio IX bakery labour claim is attributed to its excavators and is not generalised to all workers.
Source links support the written learning content. No source photographs or scans have been copied or licensed by this research task.
rights: Newly written summaries and questions. External sources linked for reference; no source images or 3D data reused.
